i0: We use ***can*** for **ability** and **possibility** now: *I **can** speak three languages.* ***Could*** is the past: *I **could** swim when I was five.* For other tenses, we use ***be able to***: *I'll **be able to** help you tomorrow.*
i1: *Can* and *could* are also used for requests and permission (*Can I…? Could you…?*). Those uses have their own page: [Requests, Offers and Permission](/blog/grammar/requests-offers-permission/).
ccb-can.s: **can / can't + base verb** for ability: *I **can** swim. She **can't** drive. **Can** you cook?*
ccb-can.b0.0.1: *I / you / he / she / we / they **can** swim.*
ccb-can.b1: *Can* is the same for every person, with no *-s*: *He **can** sing.* Not *He cans sing*. It's followed by the base verb with no *to*: *I can **swim***, not *I can to swim*.
ccb-can.b2: The full negative is written as one word: ***cannot***. In speech, *can* is usually weak /kən/ and *can't* is strong /kɑːnt/ (BrE) or /kænt/ (AmE).
ccb-could-past.t: Could and couldn't: ability in the past
ccb-could-past.s: **could / couldn't + base verb** for general ability in the past: *I **could** swim when I was five. I **couldn't** sleep last night.*
ccb-could-past.b0: ***Could*** is the past of *can* for **general ability**: *When I was young, I **could** run very fast.*
ccb-could-past.b1: ***Couldn't*** is used for both general ability and **one situation**: *I **couldn't** find my keys this morning. We **couldn't** hear the music.*
ccb-could-past.b2: Questions: ***Could** you **swim** when you were a child?*
ccb-could-past.b3: With verbs of the senses (*see, hear, smell, taste*) and *understand, remember*, we often use *could* for one situation: *I **could** see the sea from my window.*
ccb-be-able-to.t: Be able to: other tenses and after other verbs
ccb-be-able-to.s: Use **be able to** where *can* is impossible: *I'll **be able to** help tomorrow. I've never **been able to** dance. I'd like to **be able to** ski.*
ccb-be-able-to.b0: *Can* has only two forms: *can* and *could*. For other tenses and structures, use ***be able to***:
ccb-be-able-to.b1.0.1: *I**'ll be able to** see you next week.*
ccb-be-able-to.b1.1.1: *She **hasn't been able to** sleep well recently.*
ccb-be-able-to.b1.2.1: *You **might be able to** get a ticket.*
ccb-be-able-to.b1.3.1: *I'd love **to be able to** play the guitar.*
ccb-be-able-to.b1.4.1: *I enjoy **being able to** work from home.*
ccb-be-able-to.b2: In the present, *be able to* is possible but more formal than *can*: *Are you **able to** come?* = *Can you come?*
ccb-be-able-to.b3: Don't put two modals together: *I **will be able to** come.* Not *I will can come*. *You **might be able to** help.* Not *You might can help*.
ccb-managed.t: Could or was able to? Managed to
ccb-managed.s: For **one successful action** in the past, use **was able to** or **managed to**, not *could*: *The fire spread, but everyone **was able to** escape.*
ccb-managed.b0: *Could* is for **general** past ability: *I **could** swim when I was five.*
ccb-managed.b1: For **one particular** situation where someone succeeded (often with difficulty), use ***was / were able to*** or ***managed to***: *The road was blocked, but we **managed to** get home.* Not *we could get home*.
ccb-managed.b2: In the **negative**, *couldn't* is fine for both: *We **couldn't** get home.* = *We **weren't able to** / **didn't manage to** get home.*
ccb-managed.b3: Exception: with senses and thinking verbs, *could* is fine for one situation: *I **could** see the fire from my window.*
ccb-managed.w0: one success: managed to / was able to
ccb-possibility.t: Could and can for possibility and suggestions
ccb-possibility.s: **could** = something is possible (*It could rain later*) or a suggestion (*We could go to the cinema*). **can** = something is generally possible (*You can see the sea from here*).
ccb-possibility.b0: ***Could*** + base verb shows that something is **possible** now or in the future, but not certain: *Take a coat. It **could** get cold later.*
ccb-possibility.b1: ***Could*** is also used for **suggestions**: *What shall we do tonight? ~ We **could** watch a film.*
ccb-possibility.b2: ***Can*** shows that something is **generally possible**: *You **can** see the CN Tower from my window. It **can** take an hour to get there in traffic.*
ccb-possibility.b3: For future possibility, *could, might* and *may* are similar: *It **could / might / may** rain.* *Can* is not used for a particular future possibility: not *It can rain tomorrow*. See [May and Might](/blog/grammar/may-might/).
ccb-possibility.w0: a particular future possibility: could / might
x.ccb-be-able-to-b04: Not *will can*: use *will be able to*.
x.ccb-managed-b03: Not *could* for one success: use *managed to / were able to*.
x.ccb-managed-b08: One successful action: *was able to* (or *managed to*).
x.ccb-possibility-b03: *Can* isn't used for a particular future possibility.
